references.text: In [ref:Matt 27:26|Matthew 27:26], Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified at the crowd's demand, a parallel account to Luke's description of Pilate sentencing him according to their wish.
[ref:Mark 15:15|Mark 15:15] states that Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas and handed Jesus over to be crucified—the same event described from Mark's perspective.
In [ref:Joh 19:16|John 19:16], Pilate hands Jesus over to them to be crucified, which corresponds to Luke's account of Pilate sentencing him in line with the crowd's demand.

[ref:Luk 23:23|Luke 23:23] describes how the crowd, with loud cries, demanded that Jesus be crucified, and their pressure prevailed—this is the immediate cause leading to Pilate's sentence in verse 24.

In [ref:Apg 3:13-14|Acts 3:13–14], Peter reminds them that they denied Jesus before Pilate when he had decided to release him, and instead asked for a murderer—a backward reference to the unjust sentence Pilate pronounced.

In [ref:Apg 13:28|Acts 13:28], Paul says that although they found no grounds for death in Jesus, they asked Pilate to have him killed—this summarizes exactly what happened when Pilate pronounced his sentence.
[ref:Jes 53:8|Isaiah 53:8] prophesies about the Lord's suffering servant who was taken away by oppression and judgment, pointing forward to the unjust sentence Pilate pronounced over Jesus.

In [ref:Apg 4:27–28|Acts 4:27–28], believers confess that Herod and Pontius Pilate, together with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, gathered against Jesus—but that it happened according to God's predetermined plan. This shows that Pilate's sentence, though unjust, was part of God's plan of salvation.
